notes:
Based on the pages I was able to retrieve, here are verse-by-verse notes for John 18. Due to search and fetch limits, some denominational and alternative perspectives could not be fully retrieved—gaps are noted where they occur.

---

## JOHN 18 — VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### v. 1 — Jesus crosses the Kidron to a garden.

**Traditional Reading:** "When Jesus had spoken these words" refers to the Farewell Discourse (John 13–16) and the High Priestly Prayer (John 17). The group now leaves the upper room and crosses the Kidron Valley east of Jerusalem toward the Mount of Olives. John alone names the Kidron; the synoptics identify the garden as Gethsemane (Mt 26:36; Mk 14:32). The Kidron (Hebrew *qidron*, "dusky" or "dark") was a winter-flowing wadi, normally dry in summer. Spiritually significant: during Passover the brook ran red with the blood of sacrificial lambs drained from the temple altar via a channel — a vivid foreshadowing of Christ's own sacrifice. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/, https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-18-commentary)

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** Spurgeon notes that Jesus deliberately stayed within Jerusalem's ceremonial boundary (Gethsemane being within the extended city limits for Passover) rather than going to Bethany, thus fulfilling the ceremonial law. He also reflects on the symbolism of the olive trees — "twisted and gnarled as though in agony" — as suited to the Savior's sorrow. David had crossed this same brook when fleeing Absalom; now the greater David crosses to face a far greater trial. (https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons48/sermons48.viii.html, https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-agony-in-gethsemane)

**Evangelical (bible.org):** John omits the agony in Gethsemane (found in the synoptics). Throughout the Johannine Passion narrative, Jesus is portrayed not as a victim but as the sovereign Orchestrator of events. (https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

---

### v. 2 — Judas knew the place.

**Traditional Reading:** Judas "was betraying" (present tense in Greek, *paradidomi*) — John repeatedly attaches this verb to Judas to emphasize his depraved character (cf. Jn 6:71; 13:2). Jesus "often met there with His disciples," making no attempt to hide; He voluntarily went where His betrayer would expect to find Him. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-18-commentary, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/)

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** Our Lord did not need to be hunted down like a thief. When the hour came, He was in the very place the traitor could readily find Him — His cheek ready for the traitorous kiss. Jesus "went boldly" because He was willing to be taken. (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-agony-in-gethsemane)

---

### v. 3 — Judas arrives with soldiers, lanterns, torches, and weapons.

**Traditional Reading:** John uses the technical term *speira* (σπεῖραν), normally a Roman cohort of 600 men (one-tenth of a legion), under a *chiliarchos* (commander of a thousand). Some suggest it may refer to a maniple of 200 men. This force came from the Antonia fortress garrisoning Jerusalem. Alongside were *hypēretas* — officers of the temple police, drawn from the tribe of Levi, under orders from the chief priests and Pharisees. The lanterns and torches were unnecessary given the full Passover moon (the 14th of Nisan) — they expected Jesus to be hiding. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/, https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

---

### v. 4 — Jesus steps forward, knowing all.

**Traditional Reading:** Judas hoped to catch Jesus by surprise, but Jesus "knew all the things that were coming upon Him" (*eidōs panta ta erchomena ep' auton*). This foreknowledge is a repeated Johannine theme (cf. 6:6; 13:1). Jesus "went forth" — He did not wait to be found but advanced toward His captors, taking the initiative to direct danger toward Himself and away from His disciples. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/, https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18, https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-18-commentary)

---

### vv. 5–6 — "I am He" and the soldiers fall.

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus answers with *egō eimi* — not "I am He" (the "He" is supplied by translators). This is the divine name, the Greek rendering of the sacred Tetragrammaton from Exodus 3:14 (LXX). Jesus consciously proclaims His deity, echoing the great "I AM" statements throughout John's Gospel (Jn 6:48; 8:12, 58; 10:9, 11; 11:25; 14:6). When He speaks these words, the entire cohort — soldiers, officers, and Judas himself — "drew back and fell to the ground." This is interpreted as a theophany: a display of divine majesty so overwhelming that His enemies were physically powerless to stand. Adam Clarke noted: "Our Lord chose to give them this proof of his infinite power." John Trapp wrote: "Here our Saviour let out a little beam of the majesty of his Deity, and 500 men fell before him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/, https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18, https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-18-commentary)

**Evangelical (bible.org):** Though some (e.g., Leon Morris) suggest a naturalistic explanation — the front ranks recoiling and bumping into those behind — the Evangelist's theological intention is unmistakable: Jesus, bearing the Divine Name, holds ultimate power over His enemies and the powers of darkness even in this dark hour. (https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** This event illustrates a recurring pattern in Christ's life: wherever His humiliation is most evident, there His glory breaks through — born a baby yet announced by angels; laid in a manger yet signalled by a star; submitting to baptism yet hearing the divine voice; surrendering to arrest yet knocking soldiers to the ground with a word. (Cited in Enduring Word via Maclaren; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/)

---

### vv. 7–9 — Jesus protects His disciples.

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus asks again, compelling them to state their intent. Then He commands: "If you seek Me, let these go their way." This is the language of authority, not entreaty (Clarke). Having demonstrated His power, He now voluntarily surrenders Himself — and uses His authority to protect the disciples. John sees this as the fulfillment of Jesus' earlier words: "Of those whom You gave Me I have lost none" (Jn 6:39; 17:12). The disciples' physical escape prefigures the spiritual deliverance Christ would accomplish at the cross. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/, https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** In his sermon "Christ's Care of His Disciples," Spurgeon sees this as a foreshadowing of substitutionary atonement: "This was the beginning of Christ's deliverances … the picturing of the great deed of substitution whereby Christ would be able to say, 'If therefore ye seek me, let these go their way.'" He extends the principle to Providence (Christ bore the brunt so all things work for believers' good) and to Justice (Christ stood before the bar of Justice as the sinner's Substitute, and Justice accepted the substitution). (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/christs-care-of-his-disciples)

---

### vv. 10–11 — Peter strikes Malchus; Jesus speaks of the cup.

**Traditional Reading:** Only John names the disciple as Peter and the servant as Malchus. "Right ear" and the double diminutive *ōtarion* (earlobe) are eyewitness details. John alone records Jesus saying, "Shall I not drink the cup which My Father has given Me?" — linking the arrest to the Gethsemane prayer recorded in the synoptics (Mt 26:39; Mk 14:36; Lk 22:42). The "cup" is the measure of suffering and judgment ordained by the Father. Jesus rebukes Peter: the sword must be sheathed because the cross, not the sword, is the path to victory. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/, https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

---

### v. 12 — Jesus arrested and bound.

**Traditional Reading:** Two groups are specified: the Roman cohort under its *chiliarchos* (commander) and the Jewish temple officers. Jesus is bound despite having surrendered willingly. This echoes Isaac in Genesis 22:9, who allowed himself to be bound for sacrifice. Spurgeon noted: hands that healed the sick and raised the dead could certainly have broken those bonds — He remained bound only by the cords of love and submission to the Father's will. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/, https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

---

### vv. 13–14 — Jesus brought to Annas; Caiaphas recalled.

**Traditional Reading:** Annas had been high priest from AD 6–15 (deposed by the Roman prefect Valerius Gratus). Though no longer the official high priest, he was the real power behind the office — father-in-law to Caiaphas and patriarch of a dynasty that saw five sons serve as high priest. The Talmud says: "Woe to the house of Annas! Woe to their serpent's hiss!" John also reminds readers of Caiaphas's unknowing prophecy (Jn 11:49–52) — that it was "expedient that one man should die for the people." The judgment against Jesus was predetermined. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/, https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

**Evangelical (bible.org):** Why is Annas called "high priest" in v. 19? Possibly a courtesy title (like "Mr. President" for ex-presidents), or it may reflect that many Jews regarded the high priesthood as a lifetime office (Num 25:25) and refused to recognize Roman-appointed changes. (https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

---

### vv. 15–16 — Peter and "another disciple" follow.

**Traditional Reading:** The "other disciple" is widely identified as John himself (the Beloved Disciple), who was "known to the high priest" — suggesting family connections, perhaps through the fishing business supplying the priestly household (Trapp) or through priestly lineage (Eusebius, citing Polycrates, says John son of Zebedee was a priest). This connection explains how John gained access to the high priest's courtyard and brought Peter in. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/, https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

**Evangelical (bible.org):** Alternatives proposed for the "other disciple" include Judas (who had dealings with the priests) or Nicodemus (a Sanhedrin member), but the majority view remains John son of Zebedee. The term *gnōstos* in the LXX can mean "close friend." (https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

---

### vv. 17–18 — Peter's first denial.

**Traditional Reading:** A servant girl at the door (the same one John had spoken to) asks Peter, "Aren't you also one of this man's disciples?" The question expects a negative answer (Greek *mē*), making it easier for Peter to say "I am not." John may intend a deliberate contrast: Jesus in the garden said boldly *egō eimi* ("I am"), while Peter in the courtyard says *ouk eimi* ("I am not"). Peter then joins the servants and officers around a charcoal fire to blend in. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/, https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

---

### vv. 19–21 — Annas questions Jesus.

**Traditional Reading:** Annas (called "the high priest" here) interrogates Jesus about His disciples and His teaching. Jesus gives no information about His disciples — protecting them. Regarding His teaching, He appeals to its public character: "I spoke openly to the world … I always taught in synagogues and in the temple … I said nothing in secret." He demands proper legal procedure: "Ask those who heard Me." This was a valid legal point: Jewish law required witnesses to testify, not the accused to incriminate himself. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/)

**Evangelical (bible.org):** This was a preliminary inquiry, not a formal trial. The formal trial before Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin (Mt 26:59–68; Mk 14:55–65) occurred later that night, between v. 24 and v. 28 — probably illegal under later Mishnaic law since capital trials could not be held at night. (https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

---

### vv. 22–24 — Jesus struck; sent to Caiaphas.

**Traditional Reading:** One of the officers slaps Jesus for His perceived insolence toward the high priest. Jesus responds with calm dignity: "If I said something wrong, testify as to what was wrong. But if I spoke correctly, why did you strike Me?" Annas, having nothing to answer, sends Jesus — still bound — to Caiaphas for the formal trial. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/)

---

### vv. 25–27 — Peter's second and third denials; rooster crows.

**Traditional Reading:** Still warming himself at the fire, Peter is questioned again: "Aren't you also one of His disciples?" He denies: "I am not." Then a relative of Malchus (whose ear Peter cut off) says, "Didn't I see you with Him in the garden?" Peter denies a third time, and immediately a rooster crows — fulfilling Jesus' prediction (Jn 13:38). John's narrative interweaves Jesus' trial and Peter's denials, highlighting Jesus' faithful confession versus Peter's fearful denial. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/)

---

### v. 28 — Jesus led to the Praetorium.

**Traditional Reading:** "Early morning" — possibly around 6 a.m. The Jewish leaders refuse to enter the Praetorium (Pilate's residence/headquarters), because entering a Gentile dwelling would render them ceremonially defiled and unable to eat the Passover. This is a sharp irony: they scrupulously avoid ritual defilement while pursuing the judicial murder of the Son of God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/)

---

### vv. 29–32 — Pilate and the Jewish leaders; death by crucifixion foretold.

**Traditional Reading:** Pilate comes out to them and asks for the formal charge. Their evasive reply — "If He were not a criminal, we would not have handed Him over" — reveals they expected Pilate to rubber-stamp their verdict. Pilate retorts, "Judge Him by your own law." They are forced to admit: "We are not permitted to execute anyone." John sees this as providential: Jesus had predicted He would be "lifted up" (Jn 3:14; 12:32–33), indicating death by crucifixion (a Roman method), not stoning (the Jewish method). The Jewish leaders' dependence on Rome unwittingly fulfilled Jesus' word about the manner of His death. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/, https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

**Evangelical (bible.org):** The reference to fulfilling Jesus' "word" (rather than OT Scripture) is notable; the same formula appears in v. 9. The verb *plēroō* is used elsewhere in John for OT fulfillment (12:38; 13:18; 15:25; 19:24, 36), but here Jesus' own words carry prophetic weight. (https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

---

### vv. 33–35 — Pilate questions Jesus about kingship.

**Traditional Reading:** Pilate returns inside the Praetorium and asks directly: "Are You the King of the Jews?" This was the political charge the Jewish leaders had brought — a claim to kingship would be treason against Caesar. Jesus responds with a probing question: "Are you saying this on your own, or did others tell you about Me?" — testing whether Pilate has any genuine personal interest or is merely parroting the accusation. Pilate's irritated reply — "Am I a Jew? Your own people handed You over" — confirms he is a reluctant participant, but also distances himself from Jewish concerns. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/, https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

---

### v. 36 — "My kingdom is not of this world."

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus clarifies the nature of His kingship. His kingdom is not "of this world" (*ek tou kosmou toutou*) — not in origin, nature, or method. If it were, His servants would fight. This is not a denial that He is a king, but a redefinition of what His kingship entails. It is not political, military, or territorial in the ordinary sense. Jesus' kingdom operates by different means — witness, truth, and self-giving love — not by the sword. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/, https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

**Reformed perspective (Desiring God / John Piper):** In *The Passion of Jesus Christ*, Piper notes that Jesus explicitly connects the non-worldly nature of His kingdom to the fact that His servants were *not* fighting: "If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting." The way of the cross is the way of suffering; Christians are called to the same path. (https://cdn.desiringgod.org/pdf/books_pojc/bpojc_all.pdf)

---

### vv. 37–38a — Jesus testifies to the truth; Pilate asks "What is truth?"

**Traditional Reading:** Pilate seizes on the word "king": "Then You are a king!" Jesus gives a qualified affirmation (*su legeis*, "You say it") and redefines His kingship in terms of mission: "For this reason I was born and have come into the world, to testify to the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to My voice." Jesus thus connects truth not to abstract philosophy but to His own person and voice (cf. Jn 14:6). Pilate's famous response — "What is truth?" (*Ti estin alētheia?*) — is often read as cynical dismissal. He does not wait for an answer but goes out to the Jews. Yet his question, perhaps unknowingly, stands as one of the most haunting in Scripture. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/, https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

---

### vv. 38b–40 — Pilate declares Jesus innocent; the crowd chooses Barabbas.

**Traditional Reading:** Pilate announces: "I find no basis for a charge against Him" — the first of three declarations of Jesus' innocence in John's account (also 19:4, 6). Pilate then attempts a political maneuver: invoking the Passover amnesty custom, he offers to release "the King of the Jews." But the crowd shouts for Barabbas instead — described by John as a *lēstēs* (insurrectionist, revolutionary, or bandit). The irony is profound: the innocent King is rejected; the violent rebel is chosen. The one who would bring true freedom is traded for one who sought freedom through violence. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/, https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-18)

---

## DENOMINATIONAL DISTINCTIVES (Where Found)

**Baptist (Spurgeon, 19th c. Reformed Baptist):** Spurgeon's sermons on this chapter heavily emphasize *substitutionary atonement* — reading "Let these go their way" (v. 8) as a foreshadowing of the great exchange at the cross, where Christ took the sinner's place before Justice. He also stresses the *willingness* of Christ's death and the believer's security as flowing from Christ's substitution. (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/christs-care-of-his-disciples)

**Evangelical/Reformed (Desiring God / John Piper):** Emphasis on the cross-shaped nature of Christ's kingdom — the non-violent, suffering path. "My kingdom is not of this world" (v. 36) becomes a paradigm for Christian mission: not advancing by worldly weapons but by witness and suffering. (https://cdn.desiringgod.org/pdf/books_pojc/bpojc_all.pdf)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** While broadly evangelical, Guzik's commentary reflects a charismatic openness to the miraculous: the falling of the soldiers in v. 6 is seen as a genuine supernatural display of divine power through the spoken "I AM," not merely a naturalistic stumble. He also notes the conscious proclamation of deity in the *egō eimi* formula. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/)

## GAPS AND UNAVAILABLE PERSPECTIVES

Due to search and fetch limits, the following could not be retrieved in full:

- **Lutheran (LCMS, 1517.org):** No specific content obtained. Lutheran readings would typically emphasize the theology of the cross — God hidden in suffering — and Christ's passive obedience.
- **Methodist/Wesleyan (seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu):** No specific content obtained. Wesleyan readings would likely emphasize Christ's love expressed in protecting the disciples and the universal offer of truth to all who "listen to My voice."
- **Catholic and Orthodox (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org):** Not retrieved. Catholic commentary would likely note the Petrine office implications of Peter's denials and restoration; Orthodox readings often connect the garden of Gethsemane typologically to the Garden of Eden.
- **Modern Scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org):** The NET Bible notes were referenced secondhand via Precept Austin (e.g., on the Kidron and transition from the Farewell Discourse). Direct modern critical perspectives (e.g., debates about the historicity of the Annas trial, the chronology of the Passover) were not retrieved.
- **Debated Popular Modern Teachings:** No content from prosperity, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace perspectives was found on the approved sites.
